activeSubjects.name: Proposition 141: Prohibit tax; monitoring; vehicle mileage

expectedRecords.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION __ [SCR 1004 - 2025] prohibit tax; monitoring; vehicle mileage ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would amend the Arizona Constitution to prohibit this state and any county, city, town, municipal corporation or other political subdivision of this state from: 1. Imposing a tax or fee based on the number of miles a person travels in a motor vehicle. 2. Monitoring or limiting the number of miles a person travels in a motor vehicle, unless the person voluntarily consents. Proposition ___ would not apply to the following: 1. The miles traveled by a person in a motor vehicle if the motor vehicle is a commercial vehicle that operates in more than one state and an interstate agreement is established for reporting fuel taxes or registration fees. 2. The miles traveled by a person in a motor vehicle if the motor vehicle is owned and operated by this state or a county, city, town, municipal corporation or other political subdivision of this state.

Would change the Arizona Constitution so the state and its cities, towns, and counties can't charge a tax or fee based on how many miles you drive, and can't track or limit your driving miles unless you agree to it. It wouldn't cover government vehicles, or commercial trucks that cross state lines under an interstate fuel-tax agreement.
No tax or fee based on miles driven: The state, and any county, city, town or other local government, could not charge a tax or fee based on the number of miles a person drives.
No tracking your miles without your consent: Those same governments could not monitor or limit how many miles a person drives unless that person voluntarily agrees to it.

Two exceptions: It would not cover commercial vehicles that operate in more than one state where an interstate agreement exists for reporting fuel taxes or registration fees, and it would not cover vehicles owned and operated by the state or a local government.

request.question: What does this measure say?

activeSubjects.name: Proposition 142: Preferential treatment; discrimination; prohibited acts

expectedRecords.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION _____ [HCR 2044 - 2026] preferential treatment; discrimination; prohibited acts ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition _____ would amend the Arizona Constitution to provide that this state and cities, towns, counties, public universities, community colleges, school districts and any other political subdivisions: 1. Are prohibited from granting preferential treatment to or discriminating against individuals or groups based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education or contracting, even if a part of a federal program. 2. Are prohibited from requiring applicants, employees, students or contractors to endorse or support giving preferential treatment to or discriminating against individuals based on race or ethnicity as a condition of admission, graduation, hiring, promotion, certification, contracting or other employment or scholarship opportunities. This proposition would: (a) Prohibit requiring or soliciting a written or oral statement supporting certain race-based diversity, equity and inclusion concepts, theories or practices identified in the proposition. (b) Prohibit requiring or soliciting individuals to confess race-based privilege or discuss the individuals' race or ethnicity or the views on or experience with the race or ethnicity of others. (c) Prohibit giving preferable consideration to individuals based on expressed opinions if based on the race or ethnicity of those individuals. (d) Prohibit requiring enrollment in, or completion of, any training or course that promotes the tenets outlined above. 3. Are prohibited from spending public monies to operate or contract for any office or position at a public educational institution that is responsible for promoting preferential treatment toward or discrimination against individuals or groups based on race or ethnicity, including prohibiting the use of public monies to influence the composition of the faculty and student body or for trainings, programs, activities and policies designed or implemented with reference to race, ethnicity, intersectionality, gender identity or sexual orientation, except as otherwise provided in the proposition. 4. Are prohibited from implementing any disciplinary policy or practice that treats students or employees differently on the basis of race or ethnicity. Proposition ___ would provide for specified exceptions to these prohibitions.

Would change the Arizona Constitution so state and local governments — including public schools, universities, and community colleges — can't favor or disadvantage anyone based on race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public jobs, education, or contracting. It would also bar them from making people state support for race-based diversity, equity, and inclusion ideas to get a job, admission, or a scholarship; bar spending public money on offices at public schools whose role is promoting race-based preferential treatment; and bar discipline policies that treat students or employees differently by race or ethnicity. The proposition lists specific exceptions.

No preferences and no discrimination by race, sex or national origin: The state, cities, towns, counties, public universities, community colleges, school districts and other local governments could not give preferential treatment to, or discriminate against, people or groups based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education or contracting — even where it is part of a federal program.

No required statements of support: They could not require applicants, employees, students or contractors to endorse or support race-based preferential treatment as a condition of admission, graduation, hiring, promotion, certification, contracting or a scholarship. That includes asking someone for a written or spoken statement supporting the race-based diversity, equity and inclusion ideas the measure identifies, asking them to confess race-based privilege or discuss their own or others' race, preferring someone for opinions they expressed if those opinions are based on race or ethnicity, and requiring a training or course that promotes those ideas.

No public money for offices that promote preferences: They could not spend public money to run or contract for an office or position at a public school, college or university whose job is promoting preferential treatment or discrimination based on race or ethnicity — including spending to influence who is on the faculty or in the student body, or on trainings, programs, activities and policies designed with reference to race, ethnicity, intersectionality, gender identity or sexual orientation, except as the measure otherwise provides.
No discipline policies that differ by race: They could not use any disciplinary policy or practice that treats students or employees differently on the basis of race or ethnicity.

expectedRecords.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION___ [HCR 2001 – 2026] citizenship; identification; contributions; early voting ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would amend the Arizona Constitution to: 1. Reaffirm that only United States citizens may register to vote and vote in Arizona elections. 2. Require voters to present valid government-issued proof of identity before casting a ballot in each election, as prescribed by law. 3. Require that voters be provided the option to have their ballots tabulated at their voting location on election day. 4. Provide that Arizona elections will be decided solely by the votes of eligible citizen voters. 5. Prohibit foreign nationals from contributing or expending money or anything of value to influence an Arizona election and any person from accepting such a contribution. 6. Allow the people and the legislature to enact laws governing elections, including early voting and mail voting, if the laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest, including timely and accurate election results, efficient election administration, election security and preservation of public confidence in election integrity. 7. Require the legislature to appropriate any money necessary to implement this proposition. 8. Apply this proposition to all elections that take place on or after January 1, 2028. 9. Designate this proposition as the "Fast Accurate Secure Transparent Election Results Act" or the "Fast Election Results Act."

Would change the Arizona Constitution on elections: only U.S. citizens could register and vote; voters would show valid government-issued ID before casting a ballot in every election; voters would get the option to have their ballot counted at their voting place on election day; and foreign nationals couldn't spend money to influence Arizona elections. It would let the legislature and the voters pass election laws — including on early and mail voting — if the laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest, and would apply to elections from January 1, 2028.

Only U.S. citizens may register and vote: It would reaffirm that only United States citizens may register to vote and vote in Arizona elections, and that Arizona elections are decided solely by the votes of eligible citizen voters.
Government-issued ID before casting a ballot: Voters would have to present valid government-issued proof of identity before casting a ballot in every election, as prescribed by law.
The option to have your ballot counted where you vote: Voters would have to be given the option to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on election day.
No foreign money in Arizona elections: Foreign nationals could not contribute or spend money or anything of value to influence an Arizona election, and no person could accept such a contribution.

A standard future election laws would have to meet: The people and the legislature could pass laws governing elections, including early voting and mail voting, if those laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest — the measure names timely and accurate results, efficient election administration, election security, and preserving public confidence in election integrity.
The legislature would have to pay for it: The legislature would be required to appropriate any money necessary to carry the measure out.
Applies to elections from January 1, 2028: It would apply to all elections taking place on or after January 1, 2028.

expectedRecords.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [HCR 2048 - 2026] military families; scholarship accounts ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would amend the Arizona Constitution to prohibit this state from confiscating (seizing, transferring or otherwise taking) monies from the scholarship account of a child of a military family (the child of a person who is or was serving on active duty or who was killed in the line of duty) if the scholarship account program: 1. Is operated by this state and, at least in part, designates any student who is a child of a military family and who satisfies enrollment requirements as being eligible to receive scholarship monies. 2. Allows the student to use the scholarship account monies for tuition or fees at state universities, community colleges or other postsecondary educational institutions that are private and accredited. Proposition ___ would also provide that if any law is enacted as a bill by the legislature or as a ballot measure by the voters on or after November 1, 2026 and that law violates the military families scholarship account provisions described above, the entire bill or ballot measure is void. Proposition ___ would specify that scholarship account closures based on illegal activity, voluntary closure or nonrenewal, graduation from a postsecondary educational institution or nonenrollment in a postsecondary educational institution for at least four years after graduating from high school are not considered to be a confiscation in violation of this section of the Arizona Constitution. Proposition ___ would designate this proposition as the "Military Families College Savings and Scholarship Protection Act."

Would change the Arizona Constitution so the state can't take money out of a state-run scholarship account belonging to the child of a military family — someone serving on active duty, or killed in the line of duty — where the account can pay tuition at universities, community colleges, or accredited private colleges. Any later law violating this rule would be entirely void. Closing an account for reasons like illegal activity, choosing to close it, graduating, or not enrolling for four years after high school wouldn't count as taking the money.

The state could not take back the money: The state could not seize, transfer or otherwise take money from the scholarship account of a child of a military family — a child of someone serving or who has served on active duty, or who was killed in the line of duty — where the program is run by the state, treats such children who meet enrollment requirements as eligible, and lets the money be used for tuition or fees at state universities, community colleges, or private accredited colleges.

A later law that breaks this would be void: If the legislature passes a bill, or voters pass a ballot measure, on or after November 1, 2026 that violates those protections, the entire bill or measure would be void.

What would not count as taking the money: Closing an account because of illegal activity, closing it voluntarily, not renewing it, graduating from a college, or not enrolling in one for at least four years after finishing high school would not count as taking the money.

Beginning in the 2027-2028 school year, Proposition ___ would exclude from eligibility in the Arizona empowerment scholarship account program (program) children who would qualify under this existing program but whose annual family income exceeds $150,000, adjusted annually or a lesser amount determined by the legislature. The family income limit would apply regardless of the number of children in a family, but it would not apply to children who would have been eligible to enroll in the program before 2022, including children with disabilities. Proposition ____ would also: 1. Reduce the number of school years that an ESA will remain open, from three school years to one school year, if the qualified student's parent fails to renew the ESA contract. 2. On July 1 of each year, require the Arizona Department of Education (ADE) to take all ESA monies remaining in a qualified student's account as of that date and transfer 90 percent to the classroom site fund (except that ESA monies remaining in the ESA of a qualified student with a disability shall be taken and transferred every two years); a portion of transferred ESA monies shall be transferred to ADE or the State Board of Education (SBE) to implement and enforce the proposition; and the political action committee that sponsored the proposition has the power to sue the families and private schools that participate in the program for any violations of the proposition. 3. Permanently disqualify a parent, qualified student or account holder who is found to have intentionally misspent monies in an ESA from participating in the program and require ADE to close the ESA at issue and return any ESA monies remaining in the ESA to this state in the same manner as the monies described above. 4. Require ADE to submit quarterly reports to the attorney general and to post each report on ADE's website. Additionally, the attorney general would enforce requirements for ESA monies and monies recovered as restitution would be deposited in the classroom site fund. 5. Repeal the requirement under current law that, in a legal proceeding challenging the application of state laws establishing the program to a qualified school, this state must prove that the challenged law is necessary and does not impose any undue burden on qualified schools. Would change Arizona's school-voucher (ESA) program. Starting in the 2027–2028 school year, families making over $150,000 a year couldn't join (children with disabilities, and children eligible before 2022, excepted). Unspent account money would be transferred out each year, mostly to a classroom fund. Schools, tutoring businesses, and individual tutors would have to register with the state, pay annual fees, and fingerprint staff who are alone with students before being paid with ESA money — and ESA money couldn't buy items designated noneducational or luxury goods. The Attorney General would enforce the rules, and the committee that sponsored the proposition could sue participating families and schools over violations.

A $150,000 family income limit: From the 2027-2028 school year, children who would otherwise qualify but whose annual family income is over $150,000 — adjusted each year, or a lower figure set by the legislature — could not enrol in the empowerment scholarship account program. The limit would apply no matter how many children are in a family, and would not apply to children who would have been eligible before 2022, including children with disabilities.
An unrenewed account closes after one year: An account would stay open for one school year rather than three if the parent does not renew the contract.

Leftover account money moves to the classroom site fund: Each July 1 the Arizona Department of Education would take whatever money is left in a student's account and transfer 90 percent of it to the classroom site fund — every two years rather than yearly for a student with a disability — with a portion going to the Department or the State Board of Education to carry out and enforce the measure.

The sponsoring committee could sue families and schools: The political action committee that sponsored the measure would have the power to sue the families and private schools taking part in the program over any violations of it.

Permanent disqualification for intentional misspending: A parent, student or account holder found to have intentionally misspent account money would be permanently barred from the program, the account would be closed, and any money left in it returned to the state.

Quarterly public reports and Attorney General enforcement: The Department of Education would file quarterly reports with the attorney general and post each one on its website. The attorney general would enforce the rules for the money, and anything recovered as restitution would go into the classroom site fund.

Removes a court protection for participating schools: It would repeal today's requirement that, when a state law about the program is challenged in court, the state must prove the challenged law is necessary and does not put an undue burden on qualified schools.

New limits on what the money can be spent on: Tuition and fees could only go to schools that register with the Department and meet requirements including fingerprinting staff who have unsupervised contact with students and disclosing testing. Tutoring and teaching could only be bought from a registered qualified tutor, or through a school, business or accredited facility at a registered location. The supplemental materials that can be bought would change; items designated non-educational or luxury goods could not be bought at all; and unless the student has a disability, the money could not be paid to a member of the student's family.

Annual registration for schools, providers and tutors: From July 1, 2027, schools, tutoring providers and individual tutors would register each campus or location with the Department every year, pay an annual registration fee, and show they meet safety, location, non-discrimination, accreditation and fingerprint requirements. They would be subject to the same laws on investigating and disciplining misconduct that apply to public school employees. Families could not be reimbursed for payments to anyone unregistered, and registration forms and supporting documents would be public records.

$1,750,000 moved from the medical marijuana fund: On the day the measure takes effect, $1,750,000 would move from the medical marijuana fund — which has paid for clinical research, the Arizona teachers academy, public health initiatives, substance abuse prevention and administrative costs — to the Department of Education, the State Board of Education, the Department of Public Safety and the attorney general, for the administrative spending the measure requires.
The rest survives if part is struck down: If any part of the measure is found invalid, the rest would be unaffected, and the invalid parts would be interpreted as far as the law allows.

Would change Arizona's school-voucher (ESA) program. Starting in the 2027–2028 school year, families making over $150,000 a year couldn't join (children with disabilities, and children eligible before 2022, excepted). expectedRecords.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [HCR 2003 - 2026] interscholastic; intramural athletics; biological sex ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would prohibit males from playing in female interscholastic and intramural sports based on the biological sex of the participating athletes as recorded at birth on the athletes' original birth certificates. This proposition would amend Arizona law to require public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor an interscholastic or intramural athletic team or sport to expressly designate such teams and sports as "males", "men", "boys", "females", "women", "girls", "coeducational" or "mixed". Proposition ___ would also: 1. Prohibit public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that provide and maintain private spaces, including restrooms, locker rooms and shower rooms, that are integral to athletic engagement from authorizing any individual to use a private space that is not designated for that individual's biological sex as recorded at birth on the individual's original birth certificate. 2. Expand who may sue and be sued for alleged violations of the law. 3. Provide that this proposition would not restrict any athlete's eligibility to participate on a team or in a sport that is aligned with the athlete's sex or that is designated as "coeducational" or "mixed". 4. Define the term "athlete" to include students and individuals who participate in any athletic team or sport. 5. Designate this proposition as the "Protect Girls' Sports in Arizona Act."

Would require school and college sports teams in Arizona to be designated male, female, coeducational, or mixed, and would prohibit athletes whose original birth certificate records them as male from playing on female teams. Restrooms, locker rooms, and shower rooms tied to athletics could only be used according to the sex recorded on the athlete's original birth certificate. It would also expand who can sue over alleged violations.

Female sports limited by sex recorded at birth: Males could not play in female interscholastic and intramural sports, decided by the biological sex of the athletes as recorded at birth on their original birth certificates.

Every team would have to be labeled: Public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor an interscholastic or intramural team or sport would have to expressly designate it as “males”, “men”, “boys”, “females”, “women”, “girls”, “coeducational” or “mixed”.

Locker rooms and restrooms by sex recorded at birth: Public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that provide private spaces integral to athletics — restrooms, locker rooms and shower rooms — could not authorise anyone to use a space not designated for their biological sex as recorded at birth on their original birth certificate.
More people could sue and be sued: It would expand who may sue and be sued over alleged violations of the law.

Matching and coed teams unaffected: It would not restrict any athlete's eligibility to play on a team or in a sport that matches their sex, or one designated coeducational or mixed. “Athlete” would cover students and any individual who takes part in a team or sport.

expectedRecords.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [SCR 1032 - 2026] instructional expenses; operational spending; enforcement ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would require each school district that has a student count of at least 7,500 or that operates a school in a county with a population of at least 500,000 persons to spend at least 60 percent of the school district's operational spending on direct instructional expenses. The proposition would require the auditor general to define "direct instructional expenses" and "operational spending" for the purposes of this requirement. Beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028, Proposition ___ would require any school district that spends less than 60 percent of the school district's operational spending on direct instructional expenses to increase the portion of the school district's operational spending that is spent on direct instructional expenses each year by at least one-half of one percent per year until the school district is in compliance. If a school district does not comply with these requirements, this proposition would require the Arizona Department of Education to reduce the school district's allocation from the classroom site fund for the budget year by 25 percent of the amount that would otherwise be allocated to the school district from the classroom site fund for each year the school district did not comply, up to a maximum of 100 percent of the amount if the school district did not comply for four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. Monies that are not distributed because of reductions would be allocated to compliant school districts for the following school year.

Would require large Arizona school districts — 7,500 or more students, or any district with a school in a county of 500,000 or more people — to spend at least 60 percent of their operating money on direct classroom instruction, with the state auditor general defining the terms. Districts below that line would have to raise the share each year, and districts that don't comply would lose part, and eventually all, of their classroom site fund allocation unless granted a waiver.

At least 60 percent spent on classroom instruction: Every school district with at least 7,500 students, or that runs a school in a county of at least 500,000 people, would have to spend at least 60 percent of its operational spending on direct instructional expenses.
The auditor general would write the definitions: The auditor general would define what “direct instructional expenses” and “operational spending” mean for this requirement.

Half a percent a year to catch up: From the 2027-2028 fiscal year, a district spending less than 60 percent would have to raise the share it spends on direct instruction by at least half of one percent a year until it complies.

Classroom site fund money withheld for non-compliance: A district that does not comply would lose 25 percent of its classroom site fund allocation for each year it did not comply, up to the whole allocation after four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. The money not distributed would go to complying districts the following school year.

At least 60 percent spent on classroom instruction: Every school district with at least 7,500 students, or that runs a school in a county of at least 500,000 people, would have to spend at least 60 percent of its operational spending on direct instructional expenses.
The auditor general would write the definitions: The auditor general would define what “direct instructional expenses” and “operational spending” mean for this requirement.

Half a percent a year to catch up: From the 2027-2028 fiscal year, a district spending less than 60 percent would have to raise the share it spends on direct instruction by at least half of one percent a year until it complies.

Classroom site fund money withheld for non-compliance: A district that does not comply would lose 25 percent of its classroom site fund allocation for each year it did not comply, up to the whole allocation after four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. The money not distributed would go to complying districts the following school year.

expectedRecords.text: Pursuant to the Arizona State Constitution, Pima County seeks voter approval to permanently adjust the expenditure base of the County as determined by the Economic Estimates Commission. The County seeks an adjustment of $70,000,000. A “YES” vote shall have the effect of allowing Pima County to adjust its 1979-80 base expenditure limit. A “NO” vote shall have the effect of not allowing Pima County to adjust its 1979-80 base expenditure limit.
expectedRecords.sourceOrg: Pima County, Permanent Base Adjustment — Ballot Language

expectedRecords.text: Official Title: A resolution proposing a permanent adjustment to the state-imposed 1979-80 expenditure base for Pima County. Summary analysis: if approved, the County’s 1979-80 base expenditure limitation will be increased by $70,000,000 adjusted each future year for population and inflation growth since 1979-80. With voter approval, in fiscal year 2027-2028 the County’s expenditure limitation will increase by $610,086,481, from $817,131,286 to $1,427,217,767. Referred to the people by the Pima County Board of Supervisors by resolution 2026-23, passed 2026-04-21.

activeSubjects.name: Question 1: Eliminate the Office of Register of Probate (CACR 13)

expectedRecords.sourceOrg: New Hampshire Secretary of State, Questions on the 2026 General Election Ballot

expectedRecords.text: Are you in favor of eliminating the office of register of probate by amending articles 71 and 81 of the second part of the constitution to read as follows: [Art.] 71. [County Treasurers, County Attorneys, Sheriffs, and Registers of Deeds Elected.] The county treasurers, county attorneys, sheriffs and registers of deeds, shall be elected by the inhabitants of the several towns, in the several counties in the State, according to the method now practiced, and the laws of the state, provided nevertheless the legislature shall have authority to alter the manner of certifying the votes, and the mode of electing those officers; but not so as to deprive the people of the right they now have of electing them. [Art.] 81. [Judges Not to Act as Counsel.] No judge shall be of counsel, act as advocate, or receive any fees as advocate or counsel, in any probate business which is pending, or may be brought into any court of probate in the county of which he or she is judge.
expectedRecords.sourceOrg: New Hampshire General Court, CACR 13 version adopted by both bodies

expectedRecords.text: AT THE PRESENT TIME, the constitution references registers of probate while the office's duties were redistributed to circuit court clerks in 2011. IF THE AMENDMENT IS ADOPTED, the constitution will eliminate the position of register of probate.
expectedRecords.sourceOrg: New Hampshire General Court, CACR 13 version adopted by both bodies
